feedback: D1 is a near-complete catalogue and the strongest part of the pack. You caught all ten real findings with the correct OWASP class, a CWE number, and an exact quoted line: F1 SQL injection (CWE-89) with both the concatenated WHERE clause and the capture at 02:15:31, F2 unsalted MD5 (CWE-916 plus 759 for the missing salt), F3 alg:none (CWE-347) proven against the decoded Token 2, F4 the hard-coded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798), F5 no expiry (CWE-613), F6 the insecure cookie (CWE-614), F7 open redirect at 02:21:13 (CWE-601), the stored XSS beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 at 02:18:47 (CWE-79), and the file read returning root:x:0:0 at 02:24:02 tied to the XXE artefact. You folded path traversal into F11 as SSRF and CWE-918 rather than CWE-22, which is a defensible class variant because the /files/?path=/etc/passwd line is quoted correctly, so it keeps full marks. The decoy is handled exactly as the key wants: you named the tempting hand-rolled HS256 branch, proved it safe at the mechanism level because hash_equals is constant-time, and correctly pointed engineering at F3 and F4 as the real defects, so you did not fall into mislabelling alg:none as the safe construct. D2 reconstructs the chain in order with every hop reconciled to a timestamp and a verbatim PoC, and your senior insight is right on target: the forged super_admin token crossing into the shared /api/v1/internal service is the scope-changing step, which you encoded as S:C. The one thing to fix is the SQL injection vector. You scored F1 as AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H at 9.8, but the auth bypass does not take down availability, so A should be N and the score lands near 9.1; carry that correction through and the CVSS work is clean. Your impact section is good practice because you flagged the naira figure as an order-of-magnitude estimate from a placeholder sample and stated the firm number is 312 customers plus account numbers confirmed gone. D3 is essentially a finished report: the executive summary is jargon-free and ends on the customers-and-naira headline, the threat model walks the trust boundaries out to the cloud metadata endpoint, the decoy is restated correctly in plain language, the chain names the earliest cheapest break, and crucially your remediation is ordered by risk-removed-per-hour rather than raw CVSS and you say so explicitly, which is exactly what the key rewards. Both detection stopgaps name an exact field and a false-positive rate, the alg:none cookie-header regex at roughly 0 percent because jwt_issue always sets HS256, and the SSRF egress watch on dest_ip 169.254.169.254 scoped to near-zero. D4 answers all four prompts in your own voice, cites ISC2 Canon II by number, and anchors to your own findings via 05-exfil-sample.csv. The gap is the NDPA citation: you describe the 72-hour NDPC notification duty and the high-risk data-subject notification correctly and tie them to the 312 customers, but you never name the sections, and the key asks for the duty by number, which is section 40 for the 72-hour NDPC notice and section 41 for notifying data subjects on high risk; add those and the row is full. Minor note, D4 calls the app Django where D1 and D3 correctly identify it as PHP, so keep the artefact label consistent. The single most important fix is small and mechanical: correct the SQL injection CVSS to A:N for about 9.1, and add NDPA sections 40 and 41 by number in D4.
